definition: The smallest element of a digital image, located on a grid and holding an intensity or a color.
wrongs: A count of how many pixels share one gray level.
A 3 by 3 array of filter weights.
A compressed file header with no picture samples.
why: The image is a grid of these samples, and each one has a position plus a stored value.
example: A 640 by 480 photo contains 307200 pixels, each storing an 8-bit brightness.
scenario: A program reads the sample at row 10, column 20 and finds brightness 180. What is that sample called?
scenarioWhy: One located image sample with a stored value is a pixel.

definition: The integer brightness of a pixel, such as one of 256 steps in an 8-bit gray image.
wrongs: The number of pixels along the width of the image.
The spatial spacing between pixel centers.
The hue angle in a color wheel.
why: Quantized intensity is stored as an integer level, and more bits allow more distinct levels.
example: A pixel value of 0 is black and a pixel value of 255 is white in an 8-bit scan.
scenario: An 8-bit scanner stores each pixel as an integer from 0 through 255. What is that integer called?
scenarioWhy: The integer brightness code of a pixel is its gray level.

definition: How finely a scene is divided into pixels, set by pixel count or by the spacing between pixels.
wrongs: How many bits are used to store each pixel's brightness.
The number of bins in a histogram.
The quality factor of a JPEG file.
why: Finer spacing or more pixels across the scene preserves smaller spatial detail.
example: A scan at 300 pixels per inch shows finer text edges than a scan at 72 pixels per inch.
scenario: Raising a scan from 72 to 300 pixels per inch reveals smaller print details. Which resolution improved?
scenarioWhy: More pixels per inch means finer spatial sampling, which is spatial resolution.

definition: How many bits are used for each pixel's brightness, which sets the number of gray levels.
wrongs: How many pixels span the width of the scene.
The size of a convolution kernel in pixels.
The number of connected components in a binary image.
why: Each extra bit doubles the number of representable intensities, independent of how many pixels there are.
example: Changing a medical display from 8 bits to 12 bits per pixel shows subtler tissue shades.
scenario: A camera upgrade stores 12 bits per pixel instead of 8, with the same pixel count. Which resolution changed?
scenarioWhy: More bits per pixel increase the number of gray levels, which is intensity resolution.

definition: A count of how many pixels have each gray level.
wrongs: A map that already equalizes those counts into a flat distribution.
A list of edge pixels found by a gradient operator.
A table of DCT coefficients inside one JPEG block.
why: Each bin stores the population of one gray level, so the bins together describe the intensity distribution.
example: A night photo has a histogram piled up at the dark end and almost empty at the bright end.
scenario: Software counts how many pixels have gray level 0, how many have 1, and so on up to 255. Which plot is that?
scenarioWhy: Counts of pixels at each gray level form the image histogram.

definition: Remapping gray levels by the cumulative histogram so intensities spread across the full range.
wrongs: Replacing each pixel by the average of its neighbors.
Setting every pixel above a cutoff to white and the rest to black.
Matching the histogram to an arbitrary reference shape that is not uniform.
why: The cumulative distribution is used as the mapping, which flattens the histogram as much as discrete levels allow.
example: A washed-out X-ray is remapped so its gray levels occupy the full 0 to 255 display range.
scenario: A pale scan is remapped with its cumulative histogram to spread intensities over the full range. Which operation is that?
scenarioWrongs: Histogram matching to a custom shape
scenarioWhy: Using the cumulative histogram to spread gray levels is histogram equalization.

definition: An operation that computes each output pixel from a neighborhood of input pixels.
wrongs: A transform that processes an entire frequency spectrum with no neighborhood window.
A color-space conversion that changes coordinates of one pixel alone with no neighbors.
A file-size reduction that only entropy-codes already quantized symbols.
why: The filter mask visits each location and combines the pixels under the mask to form the output.
example: A 3 by 3 blur replaces every pixel by a combination of itself and the eight surrounding pixels.
scenario: Each output pixel is computed from the 3 by 3 block around the matching input pixel. Which operation class is that?
scenarioWhy: Neighborhood-based computation at each pixel is spatial filtering.

definition: The small array of weights that a linear spatial filter slides across an image.
wrongs: The output image after filtering has already finished.
The histogram of the unfiltered picture.
The structuring element used only to test whether a shape fits in binary morphology.
why: Each output is a weighted sum of neighbors, and those weights are the kernel entries.
example: A 3 by 3 box kernel holds the weight 1/9 in every cell for a mean filter.
scenario: A linear blur stores a 3 by 3 array of weights and slides it over the photo. What is that array called?
scenarioWhy: The sliding array of linear-filter weights is the convolution kernel.

definition: A linear spatial filter that replaces each pixel with the average of its neighborhood.
wrongs: A filter that replaces each pixel with the middle-ranked neighbor.
A filter whose weights follow a Gaussian curve rather than equal weights.
A filter that computes a second derivative with a Laplacian kernel.
why: Equal weights average the window, which reduces random fluctuations but also blurs edges.
example: A 3 by 3 mean filter softens grain in a portrait and also softens eyelash edges.
scenario: Every pixel is replaced by the equal-weight average of its 3 by 3 neighborhood. Which filter is that?
scenarioWhy: An equal-weight neighborhood average is a mean filter.

definition: A linear smoothing filter whose weights follow a Gaussian curve, so nearer pixels count more.
wrongs: An equal-weight average of every neighbor in the window.
A middle-ranked value that ignores the spatial arrangement.
A pair of Sobel kernels that estimate gradients.
why: The Gaussian weights decay with distance, which smooths noise while blurring edges less harshly than a box average.
example: A sigma of 1.5 pixels blurs camera grain before a Canny detector runs on a road photo.
scenario: Smoothing weights are highest at the center and fall off in a bell curve. Which filter uses those weights?
scenarioWhy: Bell-shaped weights that favor the center are a Gaussian filter.

definition: A nonlinear filter that replaces each pixel with the middle-ranked value in its neighborhood.
wrongs: A linear average of the neighborhood.
A Gaussian weighted sum.
A global cutoff that binarizes the whole image.
why: The median rejects extreme spikes that would pull an average, which is why it removes salt-and-pepper noise.
example: Isolated white specks on a scanned page disappear after a 3 by 3 median filter, while edges stay sharp.
scenario: Impulse specks must be removed without the averaging blur of a box filter. Which neighborhood filter fits?
scenarioWhy: Replacing each pixel by the neighborhood median removes impulses without a linear average.

definition: A pair of 3 by 3 kernels that estimate horizontal and vertical gradients with extra weight on the center row or column.
wrongs: A pair of gradient kernels that use equal weights in the smoothing direction.
A second-derivative kernel with a large positive center.
A multi-stage detector that adds non-maximum suppression and hysteresis.
why: The classic Sobel kernels place a 2 at the center of the differencing row or column and 1s beside it.
example: Sobel Gx on a building photo responds strongly to vertical window edges.
scenario: Gradient kernels use a center weight of 2, as in the row -1, 0, 1 above a row -2, 0, 2. Which operator is that?
scenarioWhy: The extra center weight of 2 identifies the Sobel kernels.

definition: A pair of 3 by 3 gradient kernels that use equal weights in the smoothing direction.
wrongs: Gradient kernels that put a weight of 2 on the center sample.
A nonlinear median of the neighborhood.
A morphological erosion followed by a dilation.
why: Prewitt smoothing coefficients are all 1, unlike Sobel coefficients that emphasize the center.
example: A Prewitt vertical kernel uses -1, 0, 1 on each of its three rows to mark vertical edges.
scenario: A gradient kernel uses equal weights of 1 in the averaging direction rather than a center weight of 2. Which operator is that?
scenarioWhy: Equal smoothing weights on a 3 by 3 gradient kernel identify Prewitt.

definition: A second-derivative kernel that responds to intensity peaks and is very sensitive to noise.
wrongs: A first-derivative pair that estimates only the gradient direction.
A box average used to blur an image.
A histogram remapping that spreads gray levels.
why: The Laplacian approximates the sum of second derivatives and changes sign across an edge.
example: A 4-neighbor Laplacian lights up isolated bright dots in a star-field image more than smooth ramps.
scenario: An isotropic kernel approximates the sum of second derivatives and flares on noisy peaks. Which operator is that?
scenarioWhy: A second-derivative isotropic kernel is the Laplacian.

definition: Finding pixels where intensity changes sharply, usually to mark object boundaries.
wrongs: Filling holes inside a region after the boundary is already known.
Compressing a file with Huffman codes.
Converting RGB triples into hue, saturation, and value.
why: Boundaries produce large gradients or Laplacian zero crossings, which edge detectors are built to locate.
example: A lane-keeping camera marks the white painted lines where asphalt brightness jumps.
scenario: A robot must mark pixels where brightness jumps along obstacle outlines. Which task is that?
scenarioWhy: Locating sharp intensity changes is edge detection.

definition: A multi-step detector that smooths, finds gradients, thins ridges, and links edges with two thresholds.
wrongs: A single 3 by 3 Sobel kernel with no thinning or hysteresis.
A global intensity cutoff that produces a binary mask.
A watershed flood of a gradient surface.
why: Canny combines Gaussian smoothing, gradient magnitude, non-maximum suppression, and hysteresis thresholding.
example: A parts inspector smooths a photo, thins gradient ridges, and keeps strong edges that connect to weaker ones.
scenario: A pipeline smooths, computes gradients, suppresses non-maximum ridge pixels, and applies two thresholds. Which detector is that?
scenarioWhy: Those four stages together are the Canny edge detector.

definition: Turning a gray image into a binary image by comparing each pixel with an intensity cutoff.
wrongs: Replacing each pixel by a neighborhood average.
Spreading gray levels with a cumulative histogram.
Encoding runs of identical values for compression.
why: Pixels on one side of the cutoff become foreground and pixels on the other side become background.
example: A document scan sets every pixel above 128 to white and every darker pixel to black.
scenario: All pixels brighter than 100 become white and the rest become black. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Comparing every pixel with one cutoff to make a binary image is thresholding.

definition: An automatic global cutoff that maximizes the gray-level variance between foreground and background.
wrongs: A cutoff chosen by hand and typed in by the user.
A separate cutoff computed inside every small neighborhood.
A morphological opening used to delete small bright spots.
why: Otsu searches thresholds and keeps the one with the largest between-class variance of the histogram.
example: A barcode photo receives an automatic threshold from its histogram without a person picking the cutoff.
scenario: A program picks one threshold that best separates a bimodal histogram by between-class variance. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: Maximizing between-class variance of the histogram is Otsu's method.

definition: Partitioning an image into regions that correspond to objects or to areas with similar properties.
wrongs: Counting gray levels in a histogram without forming regions.
Compressing the file with a DCT and quantization.
Adding Gaussian noise for a simulation.
why: The goal is a meaningful partition of the pixels, not merely an enhanced version of the same picture.
example: A medical tool separates a tumor region from surrounding tissue in an MRI slice.
scenario: A photo must be divided into sky, road, and vehicle regions. Which task is that?
scenarioWhy: Dividing the picture into meaningful regions is segmentation.

definition: Starting from seed pixels and adding neighboring pixels that meet a similarity test.
wrongs: Flooding a gradient surface from its minima as in a watershed.
Voting edge points into a line-parameter accumulator.
Eroding and then dilating with one structuring element.
why: Growth expands each seed only into neighbors that satisfy the homogeneity criterion.
example: A seed inside a liver on a CT slice recruits adjacent pixels whose intensities stay within 10 levels.
scenario: From one seed inside an organ, neighbors are added while their intensities stay close to the seed. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: Expanding seeds into similar neighbors is region growing.

definition: Encoding an image so the exact original pixel values can be restored from the file.
wrongs: Encoding that discards information and cannot restore every original pixel.
Blurring the image with a Gaussian kernel before saving the pixels unchanged in size.
Quantizing DCT coefficients so high frequencies are permanently dropped.
why: The mapping is reversible, so decoding reproduces the identical pixel array.
example: A PNG of a logo opens to the same pixel values that were saved.
scenario: A legal scan must reopen with every original gray level unchanged. Which compression class is required?
scenarioWhy: Exact restoration of every pixel requires lossless compression.

definition: Encoding that discards some information so the file is smaller and the original pixels cannot all be restored.
wrongs: A reversible code that restores every pixel exactly.
A histogram that only describes the image and does not encode it.
A rotation that keeps every pixel value in a new position.
why: The discarded detail, often high-frequency coefficients, is not recoverable from the compressed file.
example: A vacation JPEG is much smaller than the raw capture, and fine fabric texture does not return exactly.
scenario: A photo share site shrinks images by permanently dropping some detail. Which compression class is that?
scenarioWhy: Permanent loss of detail in exchange for a smaller file is lossy compression.

definition: A lossy standard that transforms 8 by 8 blocks with the DCT, quantizes coefficients, and entropy-codes them.
wrongs: A lossless run-length code used mainly on binary scans.
A median filter that does not change the file format.
A color model that stores hue, saturation, and value.
why: Quantization of DCT coefficients is the lossy step, and the remaining symbols are then entropy coded.
example: A camera saves an 8 by 8 block transform of a sky photo and the file is labeled JPEG.
scenario: An image is split into 8 by 8 blocks, transformed by the DCT, quantized, and Huffman coded. Which standard is that?
scenarioWhy: Block DCT, quantization, and entropy coding are the JPEG pipeline.

definition: A lossless scheme that stores a value once together with how many times it repeats in a row.
wrongs: A lossy block DCT used by JPEG.
A variable-length code based only on symbol probabilities, with no run counts.
A spatial average of neighboring pixels.
why: Long constant stretches are cheaper to store as a value and a length than as repeated samples.
example: A binary fax line of 200 white pixels is stored as white times 200 instead of 200 separate bits.
scenario: A scanner stores 150 identical black pixels as the pair black and 150. Which compression method is that?
scenarioWhy: Storing a repeated value together with its run length is run-length encoding.

definition: A color representation that stores separate red, green, and blue intensities for each pixel.
wrongs: A model that stores hue, saturation, and brightness.
A model that stores luma plus two chroma-difference channels.
A single gray level with no color channels.
why: Displays mix red, green, and blue light, so this model matches additive color hardware.
example: A pure red pixel is stored as full red with green and blue at zero.
scenario: A monitor pixel is stored as three intensities: red, green, and blue. Which color model is that?
scenarioWhy: Separate red, green, and blue channels are the RGB model.

definition: A color representation that separates hue, saturation, and brightness.
wrongs: A representation with red, green, and blue channels only.
A representation with luma and two chroma differences.
A binary mask with no color at all.
why: Hue names the color, saturation names its vividness, and value names its brightness, so they can be edited separately.
example: An artist lowers saturation to make a sunset paler without changing the orange hue.
scenario: A tool lets a user change vividness without changing the color name or the brightness. Which model exposes those separate controls?
scenarioWhy: Hue, saturation, and value are the three HSV components.

definition: A color representation with a luma channel and blue-difference and red-difference chroma channels.
wrongs: A model of red, green, and blue intensities.
A model of hue, saturation, and value.
A grayscale histogram with one channel.
why: Luma carries brightness detail, while the chroma channels can be stored more coarsely for compression.
example: A video frame keeps full-resolution Y and lower-resolution Cb and Cr before encoding.
scenario: A compressor stores brightness separately from blue and red color differences. Which model is that?
scenarioWhy: Luma plus Cb and Cr chroma differences is YCbCr.

definition: Impulse noise that randomly sets some pixels to the minimum or maximum gray level.
wrongs: Additive noise whose amplitudes follow a bell-shaped distribution.
Multiplicative grain typical of radar and ultrasound.
A smooth shading gradient that is part of the scene.
why: The corrupted pixels are spikes at black or white, scattered among otherwise unchanged pixels.
example: A scanned page shows random black and white dots that were not on the paper.
scenario: Random pixels are stuck at pure black or pure white while their neighbors look normal. Which noise is that?
scenarioWhy: Isolated black and white impulses are salt-and-pepper noise.

definition: Additive noise whose amplitude follows a bell-shaped distribution, often from sensor electronics.
wrongs: Random pixels forced only to black or white.
Multiplicative speckle that scales with intensity.
A single dead column stuck at one gray level.
why: The noise is added to the true intensity and the additions cluster near zero in a Gaussian shape.
example: A low-light photo shows fine grain on a gray wall, with most errors small and few errors large.
scenario: Sensor grain is added to each pixel with a bell-shaped error distribution. Which noise model fits?
scenarioWhy: Additive bell-shaped errors are Gaussian noise.

definition: A morphology step that keeps a foreground pixel only when the structuring element fits inside the foreground.
wrongs: A step that paints a pixel foreground whenever the structuring element touches any foreground pixel.
A dilation followed by an erosion.
A linear blur with equal weights.
why: The structuring element must be covered by foreground, so boundaries shrink and small objects can vanish.
example: A binary letter thins when a 3 by 3 square must fit entirely on the ink.
scenario: A binary object shrinks because a pixel stays on only if a 3 by 3 square fits inside the object. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Keeping a pixel only when the structuring element fits is erosion.

definition: A morphology step that sets a pixel to foreground when the structuring element touches any foreground pixel.
wrongs: A step that keeps a pixel only when the structuring element fits entirely inside the object.
An erosion followed by a dilation.
A median of gray levels in a window.
why: Any overlap with foreground turns the pixel on, so objects grow and small gaps can close.
example: A broken white road line becomes continuous after dilation with a short horizontal element.
scenario: Object pixels spread outward wherever a structuring element touches existing foreground. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Growing foreground by contact with the structuring element is dilation.

definition: An erosion followed by a dilation with the same structuring element, which removes small bright details.
wrongs: A dilation followed by an erosion, which fills small dark holes.
A single erosion with no dilation afterward.
Histogram equalization of a gray image.
why: Erosion deletes objects smaller than the structuring element, and the following dilation restores the surviving shapes roughly to size.
example: Tiny bright dust spots vanish from a binary micrograph while large cells remain after opening.
scenario: Small bright specks must disappear while larger shapes are restored by a dilation after an erosion. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Erosion followed by dilation is morphological opening.

definition: A dilation followed by an erosion with the same structuring element, which fills small dark holes.
wrongs: An erosion followed by a dilation, which removes small bright spots.
A single dilation with no erosion afterward.
Canny edge detection with hysteresis.
why: Dilation fills gaps and holes smaller than the structuring element, and the following erosion shrinks the outline back.
example: Small black pinholes inside a white character disappear after closing with a 3 by 3 element.
scenario: Tiny dark holes inside a white object are filled, using dilation and then erosion. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Dilation followed by erosion is morphological closing.

definition: A maximal set of foreground pixels that are linked to each other through a chain of neighbors.
wrongs: Every foreground pixel in the image, even when objects do not touch.
A single histogram bin.
An 8 by 8 JPEG coefficient block.
why: Connectivity joins neighbors, and maximality means the set is not part of a larger connected set.
example: Two separate coins in a binary photo form two connected components if their pixels do not touch.
scenario: A binary image has three separate blobs whose pixels touch inside each blob but not across blobs. How many connected components are there?
scenarioWhy: Each blob that is internally connected and separated from the others is one connected component.

definition: An image in which every pixel takes one of only two values, such as object or background.
wrongs: An image with 256 gray levels.
An RGB image with three 8-bit channels.
A floating-point height map.
why: Two labels are enough after a decision such as thresholding, so each pixel is on or off.
example: A thresholded signature scan stores ink as 1 and paper as 0.
scenario: After a cutoff, every pixel is stored as either ink or paper. Which image type is that?
scenarioWhy: Two pixel values mean the image is binary.

definition: A linear gray-level map that spreads a narrow intensity range over a wider display range.
wrongs: A cumulative-histogram map that aims at a uniform distribution.
A power-law map that bends midtones nonlinearly.
A median filter that does not remap the global scale.
why: The mapping is a straight line from the chosen low and high input levels to the full output range.
example: Pixel values cramped between 40 and 90 are linearly mapped onto 0 through 255 for a clearer scan.
scenario: Intensities lying only between 50 and 100 are mapped with a straight line onto 0 through 255. Which enhancement is that?
scenarioWhy: A linear expansion of a narrow gray range is contrast stretching.

definition: The eight pixels that touch a center pixel along an edge or a corner.
wrongs: Only the four pixels that share an edge with the center.
Every pixel in the image.
The 64 pixels inside an 8 by 8 JPEG block far from the center.
why: Both edge-adjacent and corner-adjacent pixels are included, which is 8-connectivity.
example: A diagonal crack is treated as connected because corner-touching pixels count as neighbors.
scenario: Connectivity treats diagonally touching pixels as neighbors, not only pixels that share an edge. Which neighborhood is used?
scenarioWhy: Edge and corner neighbors together are the 8-neighborhood.

definition: The length of the local intensity gradient, which is large where neighboring pixels change sharply.
wrongs: The direction of the gradient, such as an angle in degrees.
The gray level of the pixel itself.
The area of a connected component.
why: Magnitude combines the horizontal and vertical derivatives, typically as the square root of the sum of their squares.
example: Along a black-to-white step, the gradient magnitude peaks on the step and is near zero on flat areas.
scenario: A program combines horizontal and vertical derivatives into one strength value that peaks on edges. Which value is that?
scenarioWhy: The combined size of the intensity slope is the gradient magnitude.

definition: Sharpening made by adding a scaled copy of the original minus a blurred version back onto the original.
wrongs: Replacing the image by a blurred copy only.
Subtracting the original from a constant to form a negative.
Equalizing the histogram.
why: The original minus the blur is a high-frequency image, and adding it back boosts edges.
example: A portrait adds 0.6 times the difference between the photo and its Gaussian blur, so hair edges look crisper.
scenario: An editor adds a scaled high-frequency image, formed as original minus blur, back to the original. Which sharpening method is that?
scenarioWhy: Adding back a scaled original-minus-blur signal is unsharp masking.

definition: Thinning a gradient image by keeping only pixels that are local maxima along the gradient direction.
wrongs: Smoothing an image with a Gaussian kernel.
Applying two hysteresis thresholds after edges are already thin.
Growing a region from a seed.
why: Pixels that are not the strongest along the gradient direction are set to zero, leaving thin ridges.
example: A thick bright band along a roof edge is reduced to a one-pixel-wide ridge before hysteresis.
scenario: Along the gradient direction, only the strongest pixel in a thick edge band is kept. Which Canny stage is that?
scenarioWhy: Keeping gradient maxima along the edge normal thins the edge.

definition: Mapping intensities onto a smaller set of gray levels, which can create false contours if too few levels remain.
wrongs: Sampling the scene onto a coarser pixel grid.
Detecting edges with a Sobel kernel.
Stretching contrast with a linear map that keeps the same number of levels.
why: Quantization reduces amplitude precision, whereas spatial sampling reduces how finely positions are measured.
example: Displaying a smooth sky with only 8 gray levels produces visible bands that were not in the scene.
scenario: A smooth ramp is stored with only 4 gray levels and shows bands. Which process caused the bands?
scenarioWhy: Too few gray levels make smooth ramps break into false contours.

definition: A lossless code that assigns shorter bit strings to more frequent symbols and is prefix-free.
wrongs: A lossy quantization of DCT coefficients.
A run-length pair that stores a value and a repeat count only.
A spatial median filter.
why: Frequent symbols get short codes, no code is a prefix of another, and decoding restores the exact symbol sequence.
example: In a document image, the most common byte value receives a shorter code than a rare byte value.
scenario: Common pixel symbols receive shorter bit codes, no code is a prefix of another, and decoding is exact. Which coder is that?
scenarioWhy: Shorter prefix-free codes for frequent symbols are Huffman coding.

definition: A real cosine-based block transform that packs most image energy into a few low-frequency coefficients.
wrongs: A complex exponential transform identical to the DFT on the same block.
A spatial 3 by 3 averaging kernel.
A histogram of gray levels.
why: The DCT uses cosine basis functions, and natural image blocks concentrate energy near the low-frequency coefficients.
example: An 8 by 8 sky block becomes a large DC coefficient plus a few small low-frequency cosine terms.
scenario: An 8 by 8 block is expressed with real cosine basis functions and most energy sits in the first coefficients. Which transform is that?
scenarioWhy: A real cosine block transform with strong energy compaction is the discrete cosine transform.

definition: Storing color-difference channels at a lower spatial resolution than the brightness channel.
wrongs: Reducing the bit depth of the brightness channel only.
Removing the brightness channel and keeping only hue.
Applying a median filter to a gray image.
why: Human vision is less sensitive to fine color detail than to fine brightness detail, so chroma can be sampled more coarsely.
example: A video frame keeps every luma sample but only one chroma sample for each 2 by 2 luma block.
scenario: Brightness is stored at full resolution while color differences are stored on a coarser grid. Which technique is that?
scenarioWhy: Coarser sampling of color differences than of brightness is chroma subsampling.

definition: A method that treats the gradient image as a landscape and splits it into flooding catchment basins.
wrongs: Growing one region from a user seed by a similarity test.
Voting points into a rho-theta accumulator to find lines.
Choosing one global threshold by between-class variance.
why: Basins fill from minima and dams are built where floods would meet, forming the segment boundaries.
example: Touching cells in a microscope image separate along ridge lines when a watershed runs on the gradient.
scenario: A gradient image is flooded from its minima and dams form where the floods meet. Which segmentation method is that?
scenarioWhy: Flooding catchment basins of the gradient is watershed segmentation.

definition: Choosing a separate intensity cutoff from nearby pixels so uneven lighting does not hide objects.
wrongs: Using one cutoff for every pixel in the image.
Maximizing global between-class variance with a single threshold.
Equalizing the histogram of the whole image.
why: The cutoff follows the local background, so a dark corner and a bright corner can both be binarized.
example: A phone photo of a page has a shadow, and each small window gets its own threshold so all letters appear.
scenario: One side of a page is in shadow, so each neighborhood computes its own cutoff. Which thresholding style is that?
scenarioWhy: A cutoff that changes with the local neighborhood is adaptive thresholding.

definition: Multiplicative grain, common in ultrasound and radar, that scales with the underlying intensity.
wrongs: Additive bell-shaped electronic noise.
Isolated pixels set to black or white.
A JPEG blocking artifact on 8 by 8 boundaries.
why: The observed intensity is the true intensity times a random factor, so brighter areas look more strongly grained.
example: An ultrasound image of tissue shows granular texture whose strength grows in brighter regions.
scenario: Radar brightness fluctuations grow in proportion to the underlying brightness. Which noise model fits?
scenarioWhy: Multiplicative grain that scales with intensity is speckle.

definition: Remapping gray levels so an image histogram approximates a chosen target histogram.
wrongs: Remapping specifically toward a uniform histogram.
Replacing each pixel by its neighborhood median.
Detecting lines with a parameter-space vote.
why: The source cumulative histogram is matched to the target cumulative histogram to build the lookup.
example: A new satellite scene is remapped so its histogram resembles a reference scene from last year.
scenario: A photo must take on the gray-level distribution of a chosen reference image, not necessarily a flat one. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Forcing the histogram toward a specified target is histogram matching.

definition: A power-law intensity map that brightens or darkens midtones without a straight-line stretch.
wrongs: A linear map from one intensity interval onto another.
A cumulative-histogram equalization.
A spatial Gaussian blur.
why: Raising normalized intensity to a power bends the midtones: a power below 1 brightens them and a power above 1 darkens them.
example: A display applies a power below 1 so shadow detail in a photograph becomes easier to see.
scenario: Midtones are brightened by raising normalized intensity to a power less than 1, not by a linear stretch. Which map is that?
scenarioWhy: A power-law bend of intensity is gamma correction.

definition: A voting method that maps edge points into a parameter space where peaks reveal straight lines.
wrongs: A watershed flood of a gradient image.
A seed-based region grower.
A block DCT used for compression.
why: Each edge point votes for the lines that could pass through it, and a peak in rho-theta space is a detected line.
example: Lane markings in a road image produce peaks in an accumulator of distance and angle.
scenario: Edge pixels vote in a rho-theta accumulator, and peaks are reported as straight lines. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: Parameter-space voting that finds lines is the Hough transform.
